title: How to choose a sofa that still works in ten years
excerpt: Frame, filling, fabric. Get those three right and everything else is preference.
author: Marion Whitlock
body:
A sofa is the single most-used object most people own, and the one most often bought in a hurry. After fifteen years of making them, here is the order we would judge one in.

1. The frame decides the lifespan

Ask what the frame is made of. Kiln-dried hardwood is the answer you want. Kiln-drying pulls the moisture out before the timber is cut, so the frame does not warp or split as your house heats and cools. Particleboard and softwood frames are cheaper and will loosen at the joints inside five years.

Then ask how the frame is joined. Corner-blocked, glued, screwed and dowelled is the standard. Staples alone are not.

2. Suspension is the part nobody asks about

Under the cushions there is either webbing, sinuous springs or eight-way hand-tied springs. Hand-tied is the best and the most expensive. Sinuous springs are the sensible middle. Elastic webbing alone tends to sag first in the seat you always sit in.

3. Filling is a comfort choice, not a quality one

High-resilience foam holds its shape and needs almost no maintenance. Feather-and-down wrapped foam feels softer and more relaxed but wants plumping every few days. Neither is wrong. Decide honestly how much fussing you will actually do.

4. Fabric: check the rub count

The Martindale rub test tells you how many cycles a fabric survives before it wears. Under 15,000 is decorative. 25,000 and up is genuine family use. Performance weaves add stain resistance, which matters more than people expect if you have children, dogs, or a habit of eating on the couch.

5. Measure the route, not the room

The most common delivery failure is not the room, it is the stairwell, the lift, or the turn at the top of the landing. Measure the narrowest point of the journey and compare it to the sofa's diagonal depth. If it is close, look at modular options that come in sections.

6. Sit in it properly

Sit the way you actually sit. Slouch. Put your feet up. Lie down if that is what you do. A seat depth of 55-60cm suits most people upright; anything over 65cm is a lounging sofa and will feel wrong at a dinner party.

Get the frame and the suspension right and you can reupholster in a decade and keep the piece for thirty years. Get them wrong and no fabric will save it.

title: Five ways to use gold without the room looking like a hotel lobby
excerpt: Warm metal is a seasoning, not a main course. Here is the ratio we work to.
author: Dev Sharma
body:
Gold went from dated to essential and back again roughly three times in the last decade. It survives because warm metal does something no other finish does: it makes low light look intentional.

Keep it to about five per cent

The rule we use in the studio is that warm metal should occupy roughly five per cent of the visible surface of a room. Legs, handles, a lamp base, a mirror frame. Once it passes ten per cent the room starts reading as a lobby.

Choose one temperature and hold it

Antique brass, polished brass and champagne gold are three different colours. Mixing them looks like an accident. Pick the one that suits your light: antique for south-facing rooms that get warm afternoon sun, polished for rooms that stay cool.

Put it where hands go

Handles, pulls, tap heads, the arm of a chair. Metal that gets touched develops a patina, and patina is what separates warm metal from gold-coloured plastic.

Pair it with something matte and dark

Gold needs a foil. Deep charcoal, forest green, unpolished stone, raw linen. Against white alone it can look thin; against a matte dark surface it reads as depth.

Let one piece be the loud one

An arched mirror, a large pendant, a single brass floor lamp. One statement and several whispers beats five medium gestures every time.

title: Small apartment, real dining table: a layout guide
excerpt: You almost certainly have room. You just need the right clearances.
author: Marion Whitlock
body:
Almost every client who tells us they cannot fit a dining table can fit a dining table. What they cannot fit is the table they were imagining.

The only number that matters is 90

You need 90cm between the table edge and the nearest wall or furniture for a chair to pull out and a person to walk behind. Where that is impossible on one side, push the table against the wall and use a bench there.

Round beats rectangular under 12 square metres

A 110cm round table seats four comfortably and six at a squeeze, and it has no corners to walk into. In a tight room it will always feel bigger than the rectangle of equivalent capacity.

Pedestal bases buy you two extra seats

Four legs fix where people can sit. A single central pedestal lets you slide chairs anywhere around the edge. In a small room that flexibility is worth more than the extra 20cm of surface.

Use the light fitting to define the zone

In an open-plan room the dining area exists because a pendant says it does. Hang it 75-85cm above the table top and centre it on the table, not the room.

Buy chairs that go elsewhere

Choose dining chairs handsome enough to live at a desk or beside a bed. Then you only ever need four out, and the other two are useful somewhere else.

title: Caring for solid oak: the honest maintenance list
excerpt: It takes about ten minutes, twice a year. Here is exactly what to do.
author: Tom Ferrier
body:
Oil-finished oak is the easiest surface in your house to maintain and the easiest to ruin. The difference is about ten minutes of work twice a year.

Daily

Dry, soft cloth. That is it. Blot spills rather than wiping, because wiping spreads liquid across a wider area of grain.

Weekly

A barely damp cloth, followed immediately by a dry one. Never leave water sitting on the surface, and never use anything with silicone or ammonia in it.

Twice a year

Re-oil. Clean the surface, let it dry fully, then apply a thin coat of the same hardwax oil along the grain with a lint-free cloth. Leave it fifteen minutes, then wipe off everything that has not soaked in. Any oil left sitting on top will go sticky.

Marks and rings

A white ring is moisture trapped in the finish, not damage to the timber. Sand very lightly with 320 grit along the grain, then re-oil the whole panel rather than the spot, so the sheen matches.

Sunlight

Oak darkens with UV, and it darkens unevenly if half the table lives under a window. Rotate the piece twice a year, or accept the patina as a record of where the light falls.

title: Behind the workshop: how a chair actually gets made
excerpt: Fourteen steps, four sets of hands, and about nine hours per chair.
author: Tom Ferrier
body:
People are often surprised by how much of furniture-making is waiting. Timber has to settle. Glue has to cure. Oil has to soak in. The cutting is the fast part.

Selecting

Boards arrive rough-sawn and go straight into the rack for four weeks to acclimatise to the workshop humidity. Skip this and the joints you cut in winter will open in summer.

Milling

Each board is faced, thicknessed and squared. We cut components 10mm oversize and let them sit another few days, because releasing internal tension in timber always moves it a little.

Joinery

Mortise and tenon at every seat rail. It is slower than dowels and dramatically stronger, and it is the reason a chair survives being leaned back on for twenty years.

Shaping

The back leg is the hardest component in any dining chair, it curves in two planes and carries most of the load. It is cut on a bandsaw against a template, then refined by hand with a spokeshave.

Assembly

Dry-fit first, always. Then glue-up in one go, clamped and checked for square along both diagonals. Twenty-four hours in the clamps.

Sanding

120, 180, 240, then a light raise of the grain with water and a final 320. Four passes, all by hand on the curves.

Finishing

Two coats of hardwax oil with a full day between them, then a week of curing before the chair is allowed near a truck.

Nine hours of work spread across roughly six weeks. That is what is inside the price.

title: A layered lighting plan for any room, in three steps
excerpt: One overhead light is why your living room feels flat at night.
author: Dev Sharma
body:
If a room looks good in daylight and flat at night, the problem is almost never the furniture. It is that the room has exactly one light source, mounted in the ceiling, pointing down.

Step one: ambient

The general wash. A pendant, a ceiling fitting, or wall lights. Put it on a dimmer, this is the single cheapest improvement available to most rooms. Aim for warm white, 2700K. Anything above 3000K starts to feel like an office.

Step two: task

Light where you actually do something. A floor lamp beside the reading chair, a table lamp on the desk, a pendant over the dining table. Task light should be at or below eye level when seated, so you see the light pooling rather than the bulb.

Step three: accent

The layer everyone skips. A small lamp on a sideboard, a picture light, something low in a corner. Accent light creates the shadows that give a room depth. Two or three low-level sources beat one bright one every time.

The test

Turn everything on at night and count the pools of light. Fewer than three in a living room and it will feel like a waiting room. Five and it will feel like somewhere you want to stay.
